props.title: Deceived

sections.content: Deceived (1991) stands as a prime example of the domestic thriller wave that dominated the early 1990s, following the massive success of Fatal Attraction (1987). Goldie Hawn sheds her comedic persona to play Adrienne Saunders, an art restorer whose perfect marriage unravels into a web of deadly secrets. The film follows similar beats to other paranoid spouse thrillers like Sleeping with the Enemy (1991) and The Good Mother (1988), but director Damian Harris brings a distinctly Gothic atmosphere to Manhattan's art world setting.

sections.content: The early 1990s marked a fascinating shift in how Hollywood portrayed marital suspicion. The Stepfather (1987) had laid groundwork for the "dangerous spouse" subgenre, but films like Deceived and Shattered (1991) specifically tapped into upper-middle-class anxiety about identity fraud and hidden pasts. The art world setting wasn't arbitrary - it allowed for commentary on authenticity versus forgery, both in artwork and human relationships.

Goldie Hawn's performance deserves special attention as it marked a dramatic departure from her usual roles. Like Kurt Russell in Unlawful Entry (1992) or Steve Martin in A Simple Twist of Fate (1994), Hawn proved comedic actors could effectively pivot to serious thriller roles. The film's strongest scenes leverage her naturalistic acting style to make Adrienne's mounting paranoia feel devastatingly real. SUBHEAD: The Art World Thriller Subgenre

sections.content: Deceived fits into a specific niche of art world thrillers that includes Legal Eagles (1986) and Still of the Night (1982). These films use the high-stakes art market as both a glamorous backdrop and a metaphor for deception. Later films like The Thomas Crown Affair (1999) would continue this tradition, but Deceived stands out for using art forgery as a direct parallel to its main character's fraudulent marriage.
